All the time that the eye took in these light appearances and the brain passed these light criticisms, there was in the heart a barbaric pity and fear which men have never been able to utter from the beginning, but which is the power behind half the poems of the world. The mood cannot even adequately be suggested, except faintly by this statement that tragedy is the highest expression of the infinite value of human life. Never had I stood so close to pain; and never so far away from pessimism. Ordinarily, I should not have spoken of these dark emotions at all, for speech about them is too difficult; but I mention them now for a specific and particular reason to the statement of which I will proceed at once. I speak these feelings because out of the furnace of them there came a curious realisation of a political or social truth. I saw with a queer and indescribable kind of clearness what a jury really is, and why we must never let it go.

The trend of our epoch up to this time has been consistently towards specialism and professionalism. We tend to have trained soldiers because they fight better, trained singers because they sing better, trained dancers because they dance better, specially instructed laughers because they laugh better, and so on and so on. The principle has been applied to law and politics by innumerable modern writers. Many Fabians have insisted that a greater part of our political work should be performed by experts. Many legalists have declared that the untrained jury should be altogether supplanted by the trained Judge.

.....

Now, if this world of ours were really what is called reasonable, I do not know that there would be any fault to find with this. But the true result of all experience and the true foundation of all religion is this. That the four or five things that it is most practically essential that a man should know, are all of them what people call paradoxes. That is to say, that though we all find them in life to be mere plain truths, yet we cannot easily state them in words without being guilty of seeming verbal contradictions. One of them, for instance, is the unimpeachable platitude that the man who finds most pleasure for himself is often the man who least hunts for it. Another is the paradox of courage; the fact that the way to avoid death is not to have too much aversion to it. Whoever is careless enough of his bones to climb some hopeful cliff above the tide may save his bones by that carelessness. Whoever will lose his life, the same shall save it; an entirely practical and prosaic statement.

message.content:
As the eyes absorbed these radiant visions and the mind scrutinized their brilliance, within the heart resided a primitive blend of compassion and dread—an emotion that humanity has struggled to articulate throughout history, yet serves as the driving force behind a significant portion of the world's poetry. This sentiment is difficult to encapsulate, but one might suggest that tragedy epitomizes the profound worth of human existence. I had never been so intimately acquainted with suffering, nor had I ever felt so distanced from despair. Typically, I would refrain from discussing such somber feelings due to their complexity; however, I bring them up now for a particular purpose, which I will clarify shortly. The reason for articulating these emotions lies in the unexpected insight they provided regarding a political or societal reality. In a peculiar and almost ineffable manner, I came to understand the true essence of a jury and the vital necessity of its preservation.

Our contemporary era has been characterized by a relentless push towards specialization and professionalism. We now rely on trained soldiers for superior combat, skilled vocalists for better singing, and expert dancers for enhanced performances. This trend extends even to the realm of laughter, where we have instructed individuals to laugh in ways deemed more effective. Such principles have been echoed by numerous modern thinkers in the fields of law and politics. Many proponents of Fabianism argue for the delegation of a significant portion of political responsibilities to experts, while legal scholars advocate for the complete replacement of untrained juries with seasoned judges.

If our world operated on pure reason, one might not find fault with such developments. Yet, the crux of all experience and the bedrock of every belief system reveals a fundamental truth: the few essential lessons that one must grasp are often paradoxical in nature. These are truths that, while evident in daily life, become difficult to articulate without veering into apparent contradictions. For instance, it is an undeniable truth that those who derive the most joy are frequently those who do not actively seek it. Another example is the paradox surrounding courage, highlighting that the best way to evade death is to not fear it excessively. A person who takes risks, such as scaling a lofty cliff, may preserve their well-being through that very recklessness. In essence, the adage rings true: he who is willing to lose his life shall ultimately find it; a statement that is both practical and straightforward.
